title: What Makes Great Professional Development?
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. pushes back on the slogan that one-and-done PD never works, observing that master teachers name every conceivable format among their best professional learning experiences, from workshops and keynotes to book studies and conversations with a teacher friend. His claim is that form is not the point; substance is. He then lists six qualities great PD shares: it is clear, efficient, doable, memorable, realistically idealistic, and encouraging of thought. He distinguishes professional development from technical training, noting that real PD needs space to process, wrestle and reflect. He closes by warning against using the list as a beating stick, for oneself or for PD providers. The post is short and ends with a plug for his online course.
points: The common claim that one-and-done PD does not work is too simple, because excellent PD has come in every format; the format is not what matters.
Great PD is doable: it asks teachers to get 1-15% better this year rather than handing them 1,000 new things to do.
PD should be memorable through a simple structure, such as a short list or diagram, that lets teachers carry the ideas back to their classrooms.
Professional development differs from technical training because it must leave time for teachers to write, discuss, plan and reflect.
The six criteria are a standard to improve toward, not a stick to beat PD providers or yourself with.
quotes: Good professional development doesn't come in a single kind of package. It kills me when I hear people say things like, “Everyone knows that one-and-done PD doesn't work.

So does this mean our approach to professional development ought to follow the ol' throw stuff at the wall and see what sticks? Not at all. My point is that the form isn't the point — it's the substance.
It's clear. All the words, stories, and studies serve the message. After good PD, you see better.
It's doable. It doesn't come in and blow everything up. It doesn't give you 1,000 new things to do. It asks you to get 1-15% better at your work this year — that's it.

It's memorable. The ideas in good PD need not be over-simplified, but there's typically a simple way to carry the ideas around — a sensible structure, a short list, something in which our brains can hold what we're learning.
But professional development isn't the same thing as technical training. PD encourages us to process and wrestle and reflect; during it, we need time to write or discuss or plan.

One more thing: do not use that list as a beating stick — for yourself, if you're a PD provider, or for the person standing in front of you at your next PD experience. We all need to get better at PD.
